findings.description: This round's own fix for M3-NEW-4 (wrapping pump_resumes()'s safe_script call in an InstructionBudgetGuard, matching every other dispatch_* entry point) introduces a narrower correctness gap of its own, worth flagging even though I judge it non-blocking. Every OTHER guarded call site gives each individual callback its own fresh, full instruction_budget_: call_event_handlers constructs a new InstructionBudgetGuard inside its for-loop, once per handler; dispatch_timer's fn() call and register_trigger/register_alias's action lambdas each get their own guard per firing. pump_resumes() does not follow that per-callback pattern: it wraps its entire while-loop (client._pump_resumes(), which can drain an arbitrary number of queued coroutine.resume() calls -- one per pending client.wait_for/client.sleep continuation -- all queued during a single dispatch_line/dispatch_gmcp/dispatch_timer/etc. call) in exactly ONE InstructionBudgetGuard, constructed once before the loop starts. SPEC.md section 4 states the sandbox 'aborts any single callback exceeding a configurable budget'; a resumed wait_for/sleep continuation is conceptually a single callback resuming, and when several such continuations become resumable from the same incoming event (an ordinary, spec-legal concurrency pattern -- e.g. several client.run_test coroutines all wait_for-ing the same trigger pattern, not an attack), they are drained together in FIFO order under one shared budget. A later continuation in the same drain can be aborted with 'instruction budget exceeded' purely because an earlier continuation in the same drain already spent most of the shared allowance -- even though that later continuation's own work is entirely ordinary and would complete fine in isolation (verified: resumed alone with a fresh guard, it always succeeds). This is not a sandbox-safety regression -- total work per drain is still correctly bounded, which is what M3-NEW-4 asked for, and if anything this behavior is more conservative (aborts more eagerly) rather than less safe -- but it is a real, reproducible deviation from the 'per single callback' budget semantics SPEC.md describes, in the specific case of batched wait_for/sleep resumptions. I judge this major rather than blocking because: (1) it requires a specific concurrency pattern (multiple simultaneous waiters resolving in one dispatch, each doing non-trivial post-resume work) to manifest; (2) it fails safe, not unsafe; (3) it does not affect any exit command or existing test (nothing in the 128-test suite or the replay fixture exercises concurrent wait_for continuations this way); (4) a real fix exists and is well-scoped (give client._pump_resumes' loop its own guard per drained item, e.g. by moving the guard construction into the Lua-side loop via a small C++-callable reset function, or restructuring pump_resumes to resume one item per C++-level call each with its own guard) but is new scope I am not requiring in an already-over-budget review cycle for a narrow, fail-safe edge case.
findings.evidence: Added tests/critic/critic_pump_resumes_shared_budget.cpp (committed with this review, not wired into tests/CMakeLists.txt, following the round-1/round-2/round-3 precedent of the Critic adding a new adversarial test file for the Builder to wire in if it acts on the finding). It registers three client.run_test coroutines, each client.wait_for-ing the same pattern and then running a 4,500,000-iteration loop (calibrated against this exact build: a single fresh instruction_budget_, 10,000,000, comfortably permits one such loop in isolation -- a plain `for i=1,N do n=n+1 end` loop only starts failing once N reaches 5,000,000, confirmed by direct measurement, i.e. roughly 2 real VM instructions per source-level loop iteration -- so 4,500,000 is individually, comfortably budget-compliant). One incoming line matches all three wait_for triggers within a single triggers_.process_line() call, queuing all three resumes; the single pump_resumes() call at the end of dispatch_line then drains all three (13,500,000 total requested real work) under one shared guard/budget. Result at HEAD (2de5016), reproduced in an isolated clone: only the first continuation completes ('first:4500000' echoed); the second and third both fail with 'error resuming test coroutine: script exceeded its instruction budget (possible infinite loop)', even though each individually is well under budget. The committed test's own assertions (completed_count < 3, budget_error_seen, completed_count > 0) currently pass, documenting this exact behavior reproducibly rather than asserting it must change.
findings.spec_ref: docs/SPEC.md section 4, sandboxing ('Instruction-count hook ... aborts any single callback exceeding a configurable budget').

disputes_adjudicated.reason: Not disputed by the Builder (still escalated, ESCALATION.md unchanged since round 1). No code under tests/live/ or tests/replay/ changed between round 3 and this round. I did not spend a new connection attempt re-confirming this (see the M3-F1 finding above for why), relying instead on three independent prior confirmations (Builder, round-1 Critic, round-2 Critic, round-3 Critic) from separate environment instances, none of which the Builder has disputed at any point. This remains a genuine environmental blocker outside the Builder's or any Critic's control from inside this environment.

Genuinely resolved, independently re-verified by mutation rather than trusted from HANDOFF.md's or round 3's own claim. Built a clean checkout of 2de5016 fresh (release preset): 128/128 tests pass, including both test #118 (the round-2 ScriptEngine-level timer-bindings test) and the new test #127 (tests/critic/critic_reset_timer_binding_coverage.cpp, now wired into tests/CMakeLists.txt as the commit claims). Then, in a separate throwaway clone, mutated ScriptEngine's reset_timer binding to a complete no-op (`client.set_function("reset_timer", [this](sol::object) {});`), left tests/CMakeLists.txt as-is (both tests still built), and reran only these two tests: test #118 (the round-2 test) still PASSED unchanged against the no-op mutation -- reproducing round 3's own finding that this test never actually exercised reset_timer's effect -- while test #127 (the newly wired-in test) FAILED as expected (CHECK(f.count_fires_within(40ms) == 0): got 1; CHECK(f.count_fires_within(1000ms) == 1): got 0), exactly matching the fix's intended coverage. The mutation-check CRITIC.md mandates for this finding is satisfied by this independent reproduction, not merely by re-reading the commit message.

Resolved for what it asked: pump_resumes() now constructs an InstructionBudgetGuard before its safe_script call (src/script_engine.cpp:539), matching every other dispatch_* entry point's pattern, closing the one previously-unguarded top-level Lua entry point. Verified by direct reading and by confirming (via lua_newthread's documented copy-then-reset behavior, consistent with round 2/3's own established understanding of Lua 5.4's thread-creation path) that this guard's main effect is resetting the shared instruction_budget_remaining_ counter to a fresh full budget before draining pending resumes, rather than draining with whatever value was left over from the last guard that ran elsewhere. I did find that this specific fix, applied exactly as M3-NEW-4 asked (mirroring the other entry points' single-guard-per-call-site shape), does not by itself give per-*item* budget isolation within a single drain that processes multiple queued resumes -- see the new M3-NEW-5 finding for that narrower, non-blocking follow-on question, which is a distinct correctness concern from what M3-NEW-4 itself asked to be fixed (an unguarded entry point existing at all) and not a reason to consider M3-NEW-4 unresolved.
